publicationDetails.detailsText: WU International Taxation Research Paper Series No. 2026-04
publicationDetails.journalName: WU International Taxation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Zombie firms are firms that continue to operate despite prolonged periods of financial distress. When part of a group, such firms may serve as tax planning instruments by facilitating profit shifting or loss offsets. This paper studies the role of zombie firms in group-level tax planning by examining their response to DAC6, an EU directive mandating the disclosure of aggressive tax planning arrangements. Using firm-level data from ORBIS and a differences-indifferences design, I find that following DAC6, group zombie firms in the EU are more likely to exit the market than their non-EU counterparts. Among surviving firms, the probability of remaining a zombie declines for EU group firms. Heterogeneity analyses show that both firm location and group headquarters location shape these responses, highlighting how zombie firms are used within groups for tax planning purposes.

title: So Close and Yet So Far: The Ability of Mandatory Disclosure Rules to Crack Down on Offshore Tax Evasion
affiliations: Norwegian School of Economics (NHH) - Department of Business and Management Science, NHH Norwegian School of Economics - Department of Business and Management Science, Norwegian Center for Taxation and WU Vienna University of Economics and Business

detail.title: So Close and Yet So Far: The Ability of Mandatory Disclosure Rules to Crack Down on Offshore Tax Evasion

publicationDetails.detailsText: WU International Taxation Research Paper Series No. 2026-03
publicationDetails.journalName: WU International Taxation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the short-term effect of the introduction of the mandatory disclosure program for aggressive tax arrangements by focusing on the one introduced in May 2018 under the Council Directive 2018/288/EU (or DAC6). Employing bilateral data on crossborder deposits, we study the effect of this new disclosure requirement on cross-border tax evasion. Our results show a reduction of cross-border deposits in EU countries with a strong enforcement, captured by large monetary penalties for misreporting. At the same time, we document a relocation of income and wealth to countries with limited intermediary reporting obligation. Finally, we detect a short-term increase of USD 14 billion in cross-border deposits held by residents of countries offering citizenship/residence by investment programs, suggesting the use of these schemes as regulatory arbitrage to circumvent the disclosure mandated under DAC6. We provide timely and relevant evidence contributing to the debate on international administrative cooperation to reduce cross-border tax evasion.

title: The AGI Race and Existential Risk
affiliations: University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy, University of Chicago and Vanderbilt University

detail.title: The AGI Race and Existential Risk

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2026-71
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Concerns about the race to artificial general intelligence often assume that competition and resources increase risk by accelerating development. We study a model in which firms allocate scarce resources between speed and safety. Speed increases a firm's chance of reaching AGI first but leaves fewer resources for safety; safety lowers doom risk but slows arrival. Fragmentation increases total speed and conditional doom risk by shifting a fixed industry resource pool toward speed. The model also identifies a critical market size: below it, firms have positive expected payoff from achieving AGI, while above it, firms race even though achieving AGI has negative expected value. More per-firm resources always accelerate expected arrival, but their effect on conditional doom risk changes sign at this cutoff. Policy affects risk by changing equilibrium incentives: consolidation, resource regulation, commitment devices, and cautious public entry can improve welfare in some environments. The results show that AGI risk depends not only on technical considerations, but also on market structure, resource constraints, and institutions that shape the equilibrium allocation between speed and safety.

title: Renewable Externalities and Ancillary-Services Design in the Peruvian Electricity Market: Empirical Evidence Using Panel Data

detail.title: Renewable Externalities and Ancillary-Services Design in the Peruvian Electricity Market: Empirical Evidence Using Panel Data
detail.abstract: This paper provides the first integrated empirical evidence on three systemic externalities associated with renewable energy resources (RER) generation in Peru's National Interconnected Electricity System (SEIN) over 2016–2025, using monthly and annual panel data drawn entirely from public COES-SINAC sources. Study I estimates the Merit-Order Effect through a First-Differences model with robust standard errors (N = 119), finding that each additional percentage point of RER share in dispatch reduces the short-run marginal cost by S/. 2.72/MWh (p < 0.01; R² = 0.539), implying an annual systemic benefit of approximately S/. 600–700 million. Study II disaggregates the determinants of the Secondary Frequency Reserve (RSF) cost by technology and validates causal direction with a VAR(2), Granger tests, and impulseresponse functions (N = 95): only small hydroelectric generation (≤ 20 MW) shows a statistically significant, and reducing, effect; solar, wind, and biomass are not significant. Study III quantifies the firm-capacity deficit of solar and wind generation, which grew from 308 MW in 2016 to 1,618 MW in 2025, with an accumulated cost of S/. 130–260 million depending on the attribution scenario; the determining variable is technological composition (solar firmness factor 8.7% versus wind 25.1% in 2025), not aggregate RER penetration. The findings support the issuance of the Ancillary Services (SSCC) Regulation under Ministerial Resolution N.° 171-2026-MINEM/DM and suggest design refinements based on technology-differentiated cost-allocation factors and an articulated remuneration methodology.

title: Can Advanced Portfolio Optimization Beat Equal Weighting? Evidence from Indian Large-Cap Walk-Forward Backtests
affiliations: and

detail.title: Can Advanced Portfolio Optimization Beat Equal Weighting? Evidence from Indian Large-Cap Walk-Forward Backtests

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it does not involve human participants, patients, clinical data, surveys, interviews, or personally identifiable private information. The study uses public/free market data and reproducible analytical workflows for historical portfolio research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the authors.

detail.abstract:
This working paper examines whether advanced portfolio optimization methods outperform equal weighting in a walk-forward Indian large-cap equity setting. The study is motivated by a practical research question: do shrinkage covariance and risk-based portfolio construction methods improve historical risk-adjusted performance relative to a simple equal-weight benchmark in Nifty 50-style portfolios? The analysis compares equal weighting, a top-10 composite factor portfolio, minimum variance optimization, maximum Sharpe optimization, shrinkage covariance variants, risk parity, and hierarchical risk parity. The project uses a reproducible Python/GitHub workflow and emphasizes free-data implementation, data-quality controls, human review, and transparent limitations.

The documented walk-forward results suggest that the equal-weight portfolio remained the strongest overall performer in the tested setup, including by CAGR, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown severity, and information ratio. Risk parity was the closest advanced competitor, producing a very similar Sharpe ratio with lower volatility. Hierarchical risk parity reduced volatility but did not dominate equal weighting, while maximum Sharpe optimization appeared more fragile in walk-forward testing than in static backtests. Transaction cost sensitivity tests also supported the robustness of the equal-weight result under simplified cost assumptions.

These findings should be read as historical evidence from one documented research setup. The current analysis uses a current-constituent universe, does not yet include point-in-time index membership, relies mainly on price-based factors, and uses simplified transaction cost assumptions. The results are historical research evidence only and are not investment advice.

title: A Data-Driven Assessment of Arab Gulf Economic Vulnerability Amid the 2026 War

detail.title: A Data-Driven Assessment of Arab Gulf Economic Vulnerability Amid the 2026 War
detail.abstract:
Between February and April 2026, a joint American-Israeli air campaign against Iran drew retaliatory strikes across the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states. Global commentary settled quickly into a familiar frame, asking what the disruption meant for oil prices, shipping routes, and world supply chains. The question of what it meant for the Gulf itself, for its sixty million people and the trajectory of its development model, received far less attention. 
This monograph asks what the war revealed about the structure of the Gulf economy and where vulnerability proved greatest. It applies the Vulnerability Assessment Framework, a three-dimensional analytical tool rooted in the IPCC tradition and extended to economic systems by Briguglio et al. (2009) and Guillaumont (2010), to three foundational sectors: energy, food, and water. Across each, the framework decomposes vulnerability into exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity.
Two patterns emerge, one sectoral and one systemic. At the sectoral level, exposure is uniformly high across all three sectors. Sensitivity varies with the time each sector grants for a response, lowest in energy and highest in water. Adaptive capacity moves in the opposite direction: strongest where urgency is least, weakest where it is greatest. At the systemic level, the analysis argues that Gulf diversification ambitions are geographically constrained. Despite two decades of effort, the economic tracks built to move beyond hydrocarbons, namely finance, tourism, aviation, and digital infrastructure, rest on the same foundational geography as the hydrocarbon model itself. What the war revealed is the need for a reframing of the challenge ahead away from the familiar question of how to move beyond oil and gas, and toward a harder one. How does a state build what this study terms a geographically hedged economy, one whose resilience does not depend on the stability of the very geography it cannot leave?

title: Official Development Assistance Mechanisms in the EU's Foreign Economic Strategy
affiliations: Moscow State Institute of International Relations (MGIMO)

detail.title: Official Development Assistance Mechanisms in the EU's Foreign Economic Strategy
detail.abstract: The modern foreign economic strategy of the European Union is undergoing a profound transformation. Its specific features are determined by several key trends. First, there is a noticeable intertwining of the EU’s main areas of activity within the framework of the open strategic autonomy concept: sanctions policy, trade, investment flows, and the conclusion of international agreements are becoming increasingly interlinked. Second, the EU is attempting to combine the traditional principles of its foreign economic policy with issues of economic security, while simultaneously striving to maintain the overall competitiveness of the Union. Although the role of the European Commission in strategic planning is strengthening, limitations in the mechanisms of influence at the national level remain. Finally, the traditional importance of the value component as a tool for solving geopolitical tasks is gradually weakening, giving way to more pragmatic approaches. There is also a growing connection between security/defence policy and economic needs, so the economic dimension of security is becoming increasingly prominent. At the same time, a hybridisation of policies and a growing contradiction are observed: the course towards rearmament requires an open economy, yet the trend towards securitisation is simultaneously strengthening. The aim of this paper is to determine the place of development assistance mechanisms (ODA) in the EU’s foreign economic strategy amidst its transformation.

title: From Probabilistic Valuation Concept to Controlled Practice

detail.title: From Probabilistic Valuation Concept to Controlled Practice
detail.abstract: This paper sets out a minimum defensible control framework for the institutional deployment of probabilistic real estate valuation models. Probabilistic valuation is not only a modelling technique; in practice it becomes a controlled organisational process embedded in valuation review, NAV determination, audit scrutiny and investor reporting. The paper synthesises recent valuation standards developments and adjacent modelgovernance literature to define the minimum controls required for defensible use. These include scope discipline, input provenance, model versioning, reproducibility controls, dependency artefacts, convergence testing, validation routines, challenger review, override discipline and layered reporting. The central claim is that implementation quality is part of valuation credibility rather than an operational afterthought. A probabilistic model should be judged not only by whether its distributions appear plausible, but by whether another competent reviewer could reproduce, understand, challenge and govern the result within a formal control environment.

title: From 3D Skeleton Data to Metahuman: An End-to-End Framework of Driver Behavior Classification and Retargeting for Simulation-Based Driver Monitoring System

detail.title: From 3D Skeleton Data to Metahuman: An End-to-End Framework of Driver Behavior Classification and Retargeting for Simulation-Based Driver Monitoring System
detail.abstract: Driver monitoring systems (DMS) play a crucial role in improving road safety by detecting driver inattention and risky behaviors. Traditional DMS development relies heavily on human-subject experiments using driving simulators or instrumented vehicles to collect multimodal data, including 3D skeleton sequences. However, challenges such as limited demographic diversity, reproducibility issues, ethical concerns, and high experimental costs restrict large-scale data collection and controlled scenario generation. This paper proposes an end-to-end framework that reduces reliance on live human subjects by transforming real-world 3D skeleton data into photorealistic and behaviorally accurate virtual drivers using Unreal Engine (UE)’s Metahuman (MH) technology. The framework integrates a behavior classification model with a robust skeleton-to-MH retargeting pipeline, preserving motion fidelity while enabling customizable virtual driver appearance through MH Creator. Unlike previous DMS studies that focus solely on skeleton-based behavior classification or rely on generic motion libraries, the proposed framework couples a lightweight ST-GCN++ classifier with an automatic skeleton-to-MH retargeting pipeline derived from raw in-cabin 3D joint data. This integration supports Euro NCAP-aligned scenario design, automatic generation of animation-ready FBX clips from time-stamped CSV skeleton data, and immediate visualization in a photorealistic Unreal Engine environment. The proposed framework provides an ethically compliant, scalable, and reproducible solution for DMS simulation, evaluation, and standardized virtual driver behavior library development.

title: Continuous Model of Asymmetric Escalation: Joint Utility Optimization in the Iran-US/Israel Conflict
affiliations: IES David Vázquez and Principado de Asturias

detail.title: Continuous Model of Asymmetric Escalation: Joint Utility Optimization in the Iran-US/Israel Conflict
detail.abstract: This paper models the Iran-US/Israel coalition confrontation using a static game of continuous strategies with a quadratic-linear structure, analogous to Cournot duopoly. Unlike matrix games, the utility functions depend explicitly on both players' decision variables, allowing optimization via differential calculus. The model incorporates: (i) military capacity and increasing escalation costs, (ii) foreign aid flows as capacity multipliers, and (iii) the strategic value of the Strait of Hormuz as an asymmetric negative externality. Reaction functions are derived, the Nash equilibrium in continuous strategies is computed, and comparative static analysis is performed. Results show that current deterrence corresponds to an equilibrium of strategic substitutes where the credibility of the Hormuz threat shifts Iranian reaction curves, while external aid and marginal costs stabilize the system.

title: A Neo-Bretton Woods Institutional Framework: Mechanism Design for Hemispheric Monetary Integration

detail.title: A Neo-Bretton Woods Institutional Framework: Mechanism Design for Hemispheric Monetary Integration
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a Neo-Bretton Woods (NBW) monetary architecture for the Western Hemisphere, anchored by an American Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) whose supply is governed by a multilateral Hemispheric Monetary Authority (HMA). The framework addresses three converging failures in the current international monetary system: the unsustainable US fiscal trajectory, recurrent global financial crises with special focus on the Latin American and Caribbean (LAC) area, and the absence of a credible multilateral alternative to uncoordinated floating regimes. Drawing on the structural analogy between gold under the original Bretton Woods system and a supply-constrained digital reserve asset, the paper develops a mechanism design framework in which (i) the US dollar is maintained at a managed fixed exchange rate against the supply-constrained American CBDC within a defined band, with realignment of the central parity requiring HMA supermajority rather than unilateral US action, replacing the discretionary lever that ended the original system with an institutional fiscaldiscipline channel; (ii) selective capital flow management, enforced through blockchain smart contracts, addresses the historical "porosity problem" that undermined the original Bretton Woods system; and (iii) complementary investment vehicles channel development finance through transparent, rules-based institutions. The paper's primary contribution is to demonstrate that blockchain enforcement technology converts a theoretically well-understood but historically fragile interior trilemma position into a durable institutional equilibrium. The analysis is deliberately theoretical and pertinent quantitative benefit estimates, calibration exercises, and political-economy rationale and modeling are reserved for subsequent papers in the working series, of which this is the foundational entry.

detail.abstract: Financial instability has been documented as a correlate and amplifier of childhood family dysfunction, yet it remains undertheorized as an independent dimension of family trauma with distinct psychological consequences. This article draws on a phenomenological study examining how specific forms of childhood family dysfunction-parental alcoholism, domestic violence, emotional neglect, psychological control, and marital infidelity-influence adult marital relationships and parenting. Using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) with five married adults, the study identified financial instability as a cross-cutting theme that persisted into adulthood through hypervigilance about financial security, conflicting financial values within marriage, and anxiety in response to routine monetary activities. These patterns are conceptualized as manifestations of financial trauma: an attachment-and stress-mediated response to chronic material deprivation within the family system. The article situates these findings within attachment theory, intergenerational transmission models, and emerging financial therapy literature. It proposes practical implications for counselors, including the use of financial genograms, traumainformed financial assessment, and integrated therapeutic protocols that address both emotional and economic dimensions of family-of-origin experiences.

title: The Varoka Multiplier

detail.title: The Varoka Multiplier

detail.abstract: This paper introduces version 3.0 of the Varoka Multiplier-formally, the Varoka Compound Efficiency Theory-an eight-factor analytical framework for measuring the structural competitive advantage of emerging economies in technology-intensive production. I argue that the cost gap practitioners observe between countries like China and the United States is not a single-variable story. It is a compound. When wage differentials, currency undervaluation, talent depth, execution speed, energy cost, data liquidity, capital efficiency, and ecosystem density all act on the same dollar at once, the result is not addition. It is multiplication. The eight factors-α (wage ratio), β (PPP amplification), γ (talent density), δ (execution speed), ε (energy cost inverse), ζ (data liquidity), κ (capital efficiency), and η (ecosystem density) are each independently measurable using publicly available data. I weight the product by an output-quality adjustment Q and divide by a risk-drag denominator R, producing what I call the Net Varoka Multiplier (VM₃). Applied to the China-United States technology labor market in 2026, the framework yields a gross multiplier of approximately 17x and a risk-adjusted, decorrelated multiplier of roughly 10x meaning each dollar invested in an integrated engineering stack in China generates 10 to 17 dollars of comparable productive capacity in the United States. A parallel India-U.S. estimate (~8x gross, ~5x decorrelated) demonstrates that the framework discriminates correctly between sectors and geographies. I close with a discussion of why artificial intelligence reinforces, rather than neutralises, this compound-and what that means for the next decade of global competition.

title: Identifying relationship-level effects using covariance restrictions
affiliations: and University College London

detail.title: Identifying relationship-level effects using covariance restrictions
detail.abstract: We propose a new model in which relationship-specific effects or shocks are identified in a bipartite network under mild covariance restrictions, generalizing the influential Abowd et al. (1999) framework. For example, separate demand shocks are identified for each bank from which a firm borrows. We show how previous approaches break down when confronted with such heterogeneity, while our novel identification strategy yields a simple estimator that is consistent and asymptotically normal, under weaker network density assumptions than previous approaches. The methodology performs well in empirically-calibrated simulations. We apply our approach to identify relationship-level credit demand and supply shocks for thousands of firms and banks across nine Euro-area countries and three distinct economic episodes. We formally reject the Abowd et al. (1999) assumptions in nearly every country-period and show that within-firm/bank shock variation is of comparable scale to between firm/bank variation. We document considerable bias in Abowd et al. (1999) style estimates and associated regressions, while finding significant deleterious effects of the post-2022 monetary contraction on exposed firms. We highlight novel heterogeneity in the transmission of monetary policy.

title: Land Market Restrictions, Agricultural Productivity, and Rural Labor Markets: Evidence from Colombia's Land Ceiling Policy

detail.title: Land Market Restrictions, Agricultural Productivity, and Rural Labor Markets: Evidence from Colombia's Land Ceiling Policy
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how government restrictions on rural land markets impact the agricultural sector of an economy. Drawing on a combination of novel, detailed data on land transactions, agricultural production, and worker-level outcomes, the paper estimates how a law establishing municipality-specific limits on individual landholdings in Colombia affected productivity, land concentration, and workers' employment and earnings during the 1994-2004 period. Exploiting plausibly exogenous variation in restriction stringency across bordering municipalities, results show that municipalities with stronger restrictions had a permanent reduction in productivity and only modest reductions in overall land inequality. However, stronger restrictions also led to an increase in both agricultural wage-workers' earnings and the employment share in agriculture. To rationalize these findings, the paper develops a general equilibrium production model in which large landholders exert market power in both land and labor markets, and where the government can set limits on land accumulation. The model's predictions are consistent with the empirical findings and illustrate how restrictions can curb distortions that stem from the presence of market power but also prevent productive reallocation, with their net effects depending on initial levels of land concentration.

title: The Geometry of Optimal Delegation

detail.title: The Geometry of Optimal Delegation
detail.abstract: This paper studies optimal delegation in a canonical quadratic model and characterizes necessary and sufficient primitive conditions for three questions: when delegation has value relative to the principal's best uninformed decision, when interval delegation is optimal, and when a natural noninterval alternative-tiered delegation-is optimal. Under tiered delegation, low types receive a mandated action while higher types receive discretion over a separate interval. We develop a refined dual approach that shows that all three questions reduce to the geometry of two primitive objects: a marginal-benefit function g and a no-delegation benchmark b. Delegation has value exactly when g exceeds b somewhere on the type space. Interval delegation is optimal exactly when the region where g > b is a single interval on which g is convex. Tiered delegation arises when the convexification of max{g, b} replaces a nonconvex region by an affine segment, generating pooling and a gap in the optimal mechanism. This framework recovers several existing results originally derived using different methods and characterizes tiered delegation as a new optimal form.

title: Comparative Analysis Of Technological Innovation In Financial Service Delivery: A Case Study Of Moniepoint MFB And Traditional Banks

detail.title: Comparative Analysis Of Technological Innovation In Financial Service Delivery: A Case Study Of Moniepoint MFB And Traditional Banks
detail.abstract:
A Comparative Analysis of Technological Innovation in Financial Service Delivery: A Case Study of Moniepoint MFB and Traditional Banks investigate how Moniepoint's fintech innovations influence customer satisfaction, financial inclusion, and operational efficiency in comparison to traditional banks in Nigeria. This research aims to evaluate Moniepoint's role in enhancing financial inclusion and to explore the impact of its fintech platform on operational efficiency. Specifically, the study seeks to comprehend how Moniepoint's fintech innovations have influenced customer satisfaction, contributed to financial inclusion, and affected operational efficiency.

A random sampling technique was utilized to select a sample of 385 active Moniepoint users. A structured questionnaire containing closed-ended questions was employed to collect data regarding customer satisfaction, financial inclusion, and operational efficiency. The questionnaire was distributed via Google Forms and social media platforms, yielding a total of 200 respondents, which corresponds to a response rate of 51.95%.

The data was analyzed using a combination of descriptive and inferential statistical techniques. Descriptive statistics, such as mean, median, and mode, were applied to summarize the data and provide insights into the demographics of the participants and their perceptions of Moniepoint's fintech services. The interquartile range (IQR) was utilized to evaluate the variability within the data. Regression analysis was conducted to investigate the relationship between Moniepoint's fintech innovations and factors like customer satisfaction, inclusion, and operational efficiency.

The results of the study reveal that Moniepoint's technological advancements significantly enhance customer satisfaction (R² = 0.193, 95% CI: [0.298, 0.537]), promote financial inclusion (mean score = 4.188, 95% CI: [4.094, 4.283]), and improve operational efficiency (mean score = 4.238, 95% CI: [4.150, 4.325]). These findings indicate that Moniepoint's offerings have expanded access to financial services, stimulated economic development, and increased customers' ability to perform transactions effectively. In contrast, conventional banks are falling behind in terms of technological progress and customer satisfaction.

The findings of this study highlight the essential function of fintech services such as Moniepoint in fostering growth and progress within Nigeria's financial landscape. It is recommended that fintech companies, including Moniepoint, focus on customer-oriented innovation and invest in technologies that improve operational efficiency and encourage financial inclusion. Traditional banks should consider investing in digital transformation strategies, particularly in mobile banking and online services, to enhance customer experiences and boost operational efficiency. Additionally, policymakers are urged to create regulatory frameworks that support the growth of fintech while protecting consumer interests and ensuring financial stability.

title: Departmental Confrontation and the Coordination Failure

detail.abstract: The Irish state operates an institutional architecture under which inter-departmental coordination is not a failure of culture but a rational equilibrium produced by the rules under which Secretaries General and their officials are required to operate. The Public Service Management Act 1997 establishes the accounting officer model, making each Secretary General personally accountable to the Committee of Public Accounts for the proper conduct of their department's business. The Civil Service Performance Management and Development System measures performance against departmental rather than cross-departmental objectives. Together these instruments make data hoarding, decision-perimeter protection, and risk aversion toward joint accountability the rationally optimal response for every individual official. The collective outcome is suboptimal for the state. This paper diagnoses the mechanism, traces its expression across six policy domains where coordination failure has driven cost, delay, or analytic blindness — housing, the National Children's Hospital, MetroLink, the National Broadband Plan, EU infringement cases, the GDP-GNI* divergence — and tests the framework against a coordination success of comparable architectural scope in the Brexit response of 2017 to 2021, characterising the contingent conditions under which the equilibrium is overcome. It proposes three structural reforms supported by cross-cutting accountability infrastructure: a statutory framework for cross-departmental data-sharing duties operating beyond the existing Data Sharing and Governance Act 2019; a Cross-Departmental Accounting Officer role with statutory standing, supported by a cryptographically-verified Programme Accountability Ledger drawing on the Estonian Keyless Signature Infrastructure comparator and operating under the European Union eIDAS framework already in force in Ireland; and amendments to the Civil Service performance framework introducing weighted cross-departmental objectives at Secretary General and Assistant Secretary level. The paper identifies one constitutional question — the relationship between the Cross-Departmental Accounting Officer's direction authority and Article 28 ministerial responsibility under Bunreacht na hÉireann — as unresolved by primary legislation alone, characterises three principal constitutional paths available for its resolution, and offers the question for engagement rather than answering it in this paper.

title: One Good, Multiple Values

detail.title: One Good, Multiple Values
detail.abstract: This paper develops a compositional perspective on consumer value in which goods generate utility through multiple distinct underlying mechanisms rather than through a single homogeneous process. Building on prior work in Compositional Theory, the framework distinguishes between two broad domains of utility: Experiential Utility and Relational Utility. Experiential Utility refers to value arising from lived conditions and direct experience, while Relational Utility refers to value arising from evaluative and comparison-based processes. These domains are further decomposed into four underlying components: Relief, Comfort, Status, and Achievement. A central implication of the framework is that identical goods may generate fundamentally different compositional structures of utility across consumers. Two individuals purchasing the same product may derive value from entirely different sources, including experiential improvement, social signaling, identity expression, or internally meaningful achievement. Observable consumption behavior may therefore conceal substantial heterogeneity in the underlying mechanisms through which goods generate value. The paper integrates insights from consumer behavior, symbolic consumption, identity signaling, social comparison, and subjective well-being research within a unified compositional framework. An illustrative decomposition table demonstrates how identical goods may generate different mixtures of experiential and relational value across consumers. The framework suggests that understanding consumer behavior may require examining not only what consumers purchase, but also the distinct experiential and relational mechanisms through which those goods generate value.

detail.abstract:
This paper revisits a conceptual energy architecture originally imagined in 1985 as a youthful thought experiment concerning self-sustaining luminous systems and energy recirculation. While the original intuition preceded modern developments in photonics, thermophotovoltaics, optical cavity engineering, and photon recycling, its structural logic bears conceptual similarities to several contemporary research directions.
The proposal explored the possibility of a cylindrical luminous source surrounded by photovoltaic collectors arranged within a confined reflective environment, where part of the emitted radiation would be internally recycled while another fraction could potentially remain externally extractable.
This work does not claim perpetual motion, violation of thermodynamics, or over-unity energy production. Instead, it reframes the original intuition as a conceptual precursor to modern regenerative photonic architectures aimed at minimizing energetic losses through high-efficiency radiative recirculation.
The paper discusses:
• Photonic confinement concepts
• Photon recycling architectures
• Thermophotovoltaic analogies
• Non-equilibrium energy systems
• Radiative feedback structures
• Geometric energy recirculation
• Ultra-high-efficiency theoretical limits
The objective is not to propose a validated physical device, but rather to preserve and reinterpret an early conceptual intuition under the language and constraints of modern physics.

title: The Privacy Subsidy: Kyle's λ under Noise-Perturbed Order-Flow Observation
affiliations: The Open University of Japan

detail.title: The Privacy Subsidy: Kyle's λ under Noise-Perturbed Order-Flow Observation
detail.abstract: Privacy-preserving cryptocurrency exchanges alter what the pricing mechanism observes about order flow. We derive the unique linear Kyle equilibrium when a committed Bayesian market maker observes order flow perturbed by independent Gaussian privacy noise. The priceimpact coefficient and informed-trader strategy both rescale by a single factor in the privacy parameter, and their product is invariant. A welfare decomposition then identifies a closed-form per-period transfer from the protocol's LP pool to traders-the privacy subsidy, the break-even fee any privacy-aggregated exchange must charge. The result is the singleperiod closed-form privacy-noise analog of Loss-Versus-Rebalancing [11]. The primary application is shielded AMMs with explicit additive-noise injection (e.g., differential privacy); related designs (batched swaps, sealedbid auctions, oracle-pegged crossings) require separate frameworks that we leave to future work.

title: Governing Prediction: A Cyber Governance Framework for Accountable AI Driven Crime Prevention in Smart Urban Environments
affiliations: Guru Ghasidas Vishwavidyalaya (A Central University)

detail.title: Governing Prediction: A Cyber Governance Framework for Accountable AI Driven Crime Prevention in Smart Urban Environments
detail.abstract: Using a design science approach, this study proposes and validates a governance-first architectural response to a growing problem in urban security. Artificial intelligence based crime prediction systems are now deeply embedded within smart city infrastructures often operating as background utilities rather than visible decision systems. While these systems promise efficiency and predictive insight, they frequently operate without enforceable governance mechanisms. This misalignment has contributed to persistent concerns around algorithmic bias, opaque decision making and the gradual erosion of institutional trust in security technologies. Moving beyond technical optimization or ethical guidelines alone, we argue that these challenges demand a more fundamental shift. Crime prediction must be treated as a Cyber Governance problem. Not governance as an afterthought, but governance as structure. To support this claim, the paper introduces a cyber governed framework for AI driven crime prevention that embeds governance controls directly within the edge-fog-cloud architecture of smart urban systems. A prototype implementing the proposed governance architecture was evaluated using 15,000 real world incidents obtained from the Chicago Crime Data Portal (2026). The framework achieved 100 percent detection of invalid data (DLFA), 94.7 percent accountability attribution (AAR), and reduced compliance violations from 86.4 percent to 2.28 percent while incurring only a marginal reduction in predictive F1-score (0.782 → 0.765). Bias amplification was reduced from 1.875 to 1.047, and governance enforcement latency remained below 1 ms per event. Explainability, privacy-aware data handling and continuous auditability are treated as intrinsic system properties rather than external safeguards. By shifting attention away from predictive performance and toward governance robustness, this work demonstrates that cyber governance can be embedded without sacrificing predictive utility, offering an applied security model that prioritizes legal defensibility, democratic accountability and institutional legitimacy in contemporary urban environments.

title: Brief of Amicus Curiae Dr. Ron D. Katznelson in Support of Petitioner in Hyatt v. Squires,  US Supreme Court, No. 25-1049

detail.title: Brief of Amicus Curiae Dr. Ron D. Katznelson in Support of Petitioner in Hyatt v. Squires,  US Supreme Court, No. 25-1049

contentType.other: Filed with the US Supreme Court

detail.abstract:
The Question Presented in this case is “Whether the PTO may invoke the equitable doctrine of prosecution laches to deny a patent to an applicant who has complied with all the Patent Act's timeliness provisions.” The answer is categorically and unconditionally “No”, which applies in any tribunal, and the reason for that lies within the plain statutory text. Congress established in the Patent Act a closed and comprehensive statutory framework governing both entitlement to a patent and the circumstances under which that entitlement may be lost. The Act specifies the exclusive conditions for patentability and expressly enumerates the circumstances that result in forfeiture or loss of the patent right. By defining those conditions in detail, Congress foreclosed on any additional, judge-made grounds for forfeiture based on equitable assessments of prosecution delay. Allowing prosecution laches to extinguish patent rights despite compliance with statutory requirements improperly converts a statutory entitlement to a patent into a discretionary privilege conflicting with the law.

The same statutory design governs continuation practice. Section 120 guarantees that a continuing application meeting its exhaustive enumerated conditions “shall have the same effect” as though filed on the date of the earlier parent application. Invoking prosecution laches to deny enforceability of such applications nullifies that statutory guarantee by imposing extra-statutory timing requirements Congress deliberately omitted. The Patent Act instead facilitates prosecution of continuing applications over extended periods, recognizing that divisional, continuation, and continuation-in-part filings commonly occur across many years as inventions are refined, developed, and commercialized. These practices are not anomalies but central features of the statutory scheme, and Congress expected chains of related applications to mature at widely divergent times while retaining the benefit of earlier disclosure dates.

Congress also demonstrated that when it intends equitable doctrines to govern timeliness, it says so expressly. The Lanham Trademark Act explicitly authorizes courts and the PTO to apply equitable doctrines such as laches, whereas the Patent Act contains no comparable authorization and instead prescribes specific statutory timing rules and consequences. This contrast reflects deliberate legislative design: trademark law leaves timing issues to equity, while patent law resolves them through statute. The Federal Circuit’s application of prosecution laches disregards that distinction and inserts equity where Congress provided a comprehensive statutory regime.

Finally, the statutory continuation framework reflects the unique American “prospecting patent bargain,” which encourages early continuous disclosure of inventions’ “best mode” in exchange for allowing inventors to continue developing improvements and disclosing better implementations over time through continuation-in-part applications while preserving early priority dates. These developments frequently span many years and are expressly accommodated by the Patent Act. Treating such extended prosecution as presumptively inequitable undermines Congress’s chosen balance between early disclosure and continued technological refinement. Because the Federal Circuit’s decisions permit equitable forfeiture of patent rights contrary to this statutory structure, this Court should grant certiorari to clarify that prosecution laches has no place within the Patent Act’s closed and comprehensive framework. This brief takes no position on the patentability or the prosecution at the PTO of Petitioner’s underlying patent applications.

title: The Laffer Curve in the Lab: Review and Replication of Swenson (1988)
affiliations: University of Galway and

detail.title: The Laffer Curve in the Lab: Review and Replication of Swenson (1988)
detail.abstract: With a napkin, in 1974, Arthur Laffer sketched the 'Laffer Curve', suggesting that while tax increases might initially boost revenue, excessively high tax rates could ultimately reduce revenue by disincentivizing economic activity. This paper examines this concept through a replication of Swenson's (1988) laboratory experiment, the seminal study of this theory. In this experiment, participants go through a real-effort task with varying tax rates. However, we do not replicate Swenson's (1988) findings. Instead of observing a decline in effort at higher tax rates, we found that participants increased their effort provision as tax rates rose. This result indicates that, within our experimental setting, the predicted disincentive effect of high tax rates on labor supply was not observed. Our study highlights the complexity of individual responses to taxation and calls for further replications to set the definitive impact of raising tax rates on tax revenues and effort.

title: Multi-Year Droughts and Their Compounding Economic Impacts in Europe
affiliations: , RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment, Potsdam University and RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment

detail.title: Multi-Year Droughts and Their Compounding Economic Impacts in Europe
detail.abstract: Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of droughts, with unprecedented records broken in Europe. While the direct impacts on agricultural output and water availability are well documented, their medium and long-term economic consequences across multiple economic sectors remain underexplored. We investigate the persistent and compounding nature of economic responses to drought across multiple sectors in Europe. We use high-resolution economic (NUTS3) and climate data (EOBS) to capture the fine-grained patterns of drought exposure and socioeconomic vulnerabilities across multiple multiscalar drought indicators with different accumulation scales. Distributed lag fixed-effects models reveal negative impacts of drought exposure on production, investment, migration, and employment, which accumulate over multiple years following exposure. Impacts on agriculture are high but short-lived, whereas they persist and accumulate in manufacturing, especially construction, and are weaker and more attenuated in services. Evaluating the recent extreme multi-year drought of 2015-2018, we find cumulative impacts of -2.75% on GDP per capita growth, and estimate that it would rise to -5.23% under a scenario of  2°C global warming, driven by regional warming and drying.

title: Capital Market Assumptions And Strategic Asset Allocation Using Multi Asset Tradable Factors
affiliations: LGT Bank (Schweiz) AG, LGT Bank (Schweiz) AG and LGT Private Bank APAC

detail.title: Capital Market Assumptions And Strategic Asset Allocation Using Multi Asset Tradable Factors
detail.abstract:
Capital market assumptions (CMAs) provide key inputs for strategic asset allocation, yet the methodologies most commonly used in institutional practice---building-block decompositions of the Grinold-Kroner type and qualitative factor mappings---share two structural weaknesses that affect every SAA decision they inform. First, they produce asset-level expected returns that are inconsistent with the factor structure of the risk model used in mean-variance optimization. Second, they require long history to reduce estimation error.

We develop the Multi-Asset Tradable Factors framework for CMA estimation, termed MATF-CMA, which addresses both weaknesses by construction. Each asset's expected return is constructed as the product of asset factor loadings estimated by Hierarchical Clustering Group Lasso (HCGL) and the vector of risk premia for nine tradable factors including Equity, Rates, Credit, Carry, Inflation, Commodities, Private Equity, Rates Volatility, and FX. The same loading matrix enters the covariance model, ensuring alpha-beta consistency. Architecturally, MATF-CMA is a forward-looking, valuation-aware alternative to Black-Litterman architecture: it retains the three-pillar structure - structural prior, view mechanism, risk-model coherence - but replaces the market-cap-derived equilibrium prior with a factor-decomposition prior derived from market-observable risk premia. 

As a secondary contribution, we introduce a model-independent diagnostic for measuring alpha-beta consistency violation under any CMA construction against any factor or covariance risk model.

detail.abstract: We examine recent changes in stock market participation using newly available survey data from eleven euro area countries over the period 2020–2024. The evidence points to substantial turnover, with around 10% of non-stockholders entering the market each year, and more than 20% of stockholders exiting. New entrants tend to have lower education, income, financial literacy, and risk tolerance than established investors, indicating a shift in the composition of market participants. We also highlight the growing importance of cryptocurrency investments among retail investors. Overall, these findings shed new light on evolving household financial behavior and its implications for market participation and financial stability.

title: Data Privacy and Surveillance: A Shariah and Ijtihadic Analysis
affiliations: Superior University

detail.title: Data Privacy and Surveillance: A Shariah and Ijtihadic Analysis
detail.abstract:
Data privacy and surveillance are now among the most important ethical and legal issues of the digital age. Today, modern technology collects, saves, studies, and shares people’s personal information on a very large scale. Mobile phones, social media, biometric systems, CCTV cameras, artificial intelligence, and online transactions have made human life closely connected with data. From a Shariah point of view, this raises some important questions:

  • Does personal data relate to a person’s dignity and trust?
  •  Is surveillance a type of forbidden spying?
  •  Can governments monitor people for security reasons?
  • Can companies collect people’s data to make profit?
  •  What limits should Islamic law place on digital monitoring?
  • This article argues that Islam strongly protects privacy, human dignity, personal honor, confidentiality, and freedom from unnecessary spying. At the same time, Shariah also accepts that in some limited and controlled situations, surveillance may be allowed. For example, it may be permitted to protect public interest, prevent harm, establish justice, or maintain security.
  • Therefore, the Islamic approach is balanced. It does not support complete privacy without responsibility, and it also does not allow unlimited surveillance in the name of security. Instead, Islam provides a moral and legal framework based on hurmah (sanctity), amanah (trust), ‘adl (justice), maslahah (public interest), darurah (necessity), and daf‘ al-darar (prevention and removal of harm).

title: Trade Barriers and Productivity Shocks: The Dual Drivers of Pandemic-Control-Induced Economic Disruptions

detail.title: Trade Barriers and Productivity Shocks: The Dual Drivers of Pandemic-Control-Induced Economic Disruptions
detail.abstract: The effects of strict pandemic control measures have already been extensively studied. Compared with the existing literature, this paper uses a structural framework to jointly evaluate and compare global economic impacts through both trade frictions and productivity shocks. By mapping structural gravity estimates into trade costs and productivity shocks, we find that global welfare contraction was overwhelmingly dictated by the productivity effect rather than trade costs. Specifically, productivity disruptions accounted for 73% to 89% of total welfare impact, with domestic shocks explaining nearly 95% of losses in large economies. These results suggest that both productivity shocks and trade costs shocks jointly shape the overall welfare effects, with supply-side forces playing a dominant role.

detail.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) with advanced business analytics represents a transformative paradigm shift in how organizations manage financial risk and optimize supply chain operations. This paper presents a comprehensive data-driven framework that unifies edge-layer sensor intelligence, cloud-based predictive analytics, and real-time decision engines to address critical vulnerabilities in financial exposure quantification and logistics network efficiency. Leveraging heterogeneous IoT data streams-spanning inventory telemetry, transactional ledgers, logistics GPS traces, and market volatility indices-the proposed framework employs an ensemble of machine learning architectures including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM), Bidirectional Transformers, and stochastic Monte Carlo simulation to generate high-fidelity risk forecasts and supply chain prescriptions. Experimental evaluation was conducted on a curated multi-domain dataset comprising 148,000 timestamped records drawn from manufacturing, retail, and financial services sectors. Results demonstrate that the AIoTintegrated pipeline achieves a mean prediction accuracy of 94.7% for default risk classification (AUC-ROC = 0.961), reduces supply chain disruption detection latency by 67.3% compared to conventional SCADA-based monitoring, and yields a 23.8% reduction in average inventory holding cost under stochastic demand scenarios. The framework further incorporates federated learning protocols to preserve data privacy across enterprise boundaries. These findings establish a rigorous empirical basis for deploying AIoT-driven analytics in highstakes operational environments, contributing a replicable methodological template for researchers and practitioners at the intersection of intelligent systems, operations research, and risk governance.

detail.abstract:
This article offers a ruralist critique of the hyper-partisan redistricting phenomenon initiated in mid-2025 when Texas undertook reapportionment with the express purpose of garnering more Republican seats in the U.S. House of Representatives.  The focus here is how California’s equally partisan response—the Proposition 50 ballot initiative passed in November 2025—is undermining rural representation by tethering inland rural counties in far northern California to the urbanized Bay Area.  While this article examines and highlights the California example, the recent abandonment of redistricting best practices in favor of a no-holds-barred arms race raises concerns across the nation, including where urban voters are being used to dilute rural representation—and vice versa.  I ultimately call for greater attention to—and protection of—rural places as communities of interest in redistricting practice. 

The article begins by surveying the literature on rural-urban political polarization and the emerging force of rural identity to inform a discussion of how these are reflected in California’s two most northerly districts, CA-01 and CA-02, whose counties were reshuffled by the Proposition 50 map.  I also detail the likely changes in representation that will be wrought by the new map in far northern California.  Two examples illustrate the disconnect between the values and priorities of inland California, on the one hand, and those of coastal, urban residents on the other.  The first is legal protection of gray wolves, which are decimating livestock and undermining rancher livelihoods in the rural north state.  The second is state regulation deterring use of internal combustion engines and promoting electric vehicles.  These policies are often not feasible in rural far northern California, where vast distances must be traversed and the charging infrastructure is poor.  I then provide a brief primer on rural places as communities of interest in redistricting law before concluding with thoughts on how these recent events undermine democratic accountability and risk greater rural voter alienation and resentment.

This article, written for the Maine Law Review symposium on “Rural Legal Perspectives:  Challenges and Opportunities,” was in the final stages of production when the U.S. Supreme Court decided Louisiana v. Callais in late April 2026.  The further round of gerrymandering prompted by that decision is thus not addressed here.

detail.abstract: India's journey toward becoming a developed nation by 2047, envisioned under the national resolve of Viksit Bharat, rests centrally on its capacity to close the infrastructure gap that still separates urban and rural citizens. While metropolitan regions have surged ahead with expressways, metro systems, digital networks and world-class logistics, a significant proportion of rural India continues to face deficits in last-mile road connectivity, cold-chain storage, reliable power, piped water, affordable healthcare and digital access. This paper argues that closing this divide within the next two decades requires not merely higher public expenditure but a structural redesign of the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) framework so that it becomes genuinely viable in low-density, low-revenue geographies. Drawing on secondary data from the Reserve Bank of India, NITI Aayog, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, and evaluation studies of flagship schemes such as Bharatmala, PMGSY, PM Gati Shakti, Jal Jeevan Mission, Saubhagya, BharatNet and the Smart Cities Mission, the study identifies risk-allocation asymmetries, financing bottlenecks, weak institutional capacity at sub-national levels and dispute-resolution delays as the principal constraints on rural PPP uptake. It proposes a seven-pillar reform framework covering viability gap financing, hybrid annuity contracts for social infrastructure, a dedicated Rural Infrastructure PPP Authority, blended finance through multilateral and pension capital, digital project preparation facilities, community accountability mechanisms, and performance-linked federal transfers. The paper concludes that a calibrated PPP reform agenda, anchored in the principles of cooperative federalism and Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas, Sabka Prayas, can transform rural India from an infrastructure deficit region into a productive engine of the Viksit Bharat vision.

detail.abstract: South Asia is uniquely vulnerable to climate-induced and tectonic hazards due to the convergence of active lithospheric plates, monsoonal precipitation patterns, and dense coastal catchments. Standard deterministic models are frequently limited by severe transboundary data sharing silos, high computational overhead, and sparse in-situ monitoring networks. Over the period 2020-2025, data-driven machine learning and deep learning architectures have emerged as alternative paradigms capable of extracting complex, non-linear relationships from heterogeneous environmental catalogs. This paper presents a systematic survey of 42 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025 across four primary hazard domains: floods, cyclones, earthquakes, and landslides. The synthesized findings indicate that while ensemble gradient-boosting architectures achieve robust predictive performance for water level regression (R 2 > 0.98) under gauged conditions, their performance degrades significantly in ungauged domains (R 2 = 0.72-0.78). For tropical storm intensity estimation, ConvLSTM networks integrated with spatial feature extractors yield binary classification accuracies up to 99.16% under optimal sampling. Landslide susceptibility mapping, optimized via national geomorphic inventories, yields area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) metrics up to 0.93. Conversely, seismic prediction remains the most constrained hazard domain, with temporal validation protocols bounding performance at an AUC of 0.87. This survey conducts a validation integrity audit, revealing that 37.5% of evaluated seismic papers reporting accuracies above 95% suffer from data leakage due to flawed random splitting protocols. Finally, the survey outlines key operational barriersincluding explainability deficits and transboundary data blockages-and provides a priority roadmap for the development of deployable early warning architectures.

title: Interpretive Stabilization After Chevron: Loper Bright and the Transformation of the Administrative State

detail.title: Interpretive Stabilization After Chevron: Loper Bright and the Transformation of the Administrative State
detail.abstract:
Chevron deference long structured the allocation of authority over statutory meaning in American administrative law. It directed courts to defer to reasonable agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes. The Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo constitutes a structural break from this framework, restoring independent judicial judgment as the governing principle of statutory interpretation and reasserting the primacy of the Article III judiciary. This Article argues that the end of Chevron does not merely reallocate authority over legal meaning, but transforms the mechanism through which statutory meaning stabilizes over time. This shift reflects an emerging theory of intertemporal stabilization of legal meaning. In this framework, the post-Chevron administrative state is evolving toward a precedent-centered model.

In this emerging order, legal meaning is less dependent on agency recalibration. Rather, legal meaning undergoes doctrinal crystallization through the accumulation of judicial decisions. This transition does not produce instability. Instead, it initiates a structural transition in how legal meaning stabilizes over time.

Statutory meaning accordingly develops through the accumulation of binding judicial precedent rather than iterative administrative reinterpretation. Integrating administrative law doctrine, constitutional structure, and institutional economics, this transformation operates through three core mechanisms: the displacement of agency reinterpretation by judicial precedent, the disciplining effect of stare decisis, and the reconfiguration of agency expertise as persuasive rather than binding authority. It further examines the systemic implications of this shift, including a potential reduction in the "regulatory risk premium" associated with electoral cycles, increased litigation during transitional periods, and new constraints on legislative and executive behavior. By reframing the post-Chevron debate around temporal stability rather than institutional competition, this Article offers a new conceptual framework for understanding the future trajectory of the administrative state.

detail.abstract: We introduce Scheduled Coordination Density (SCD), an ex-ante measure of how much publicly scheduled institutional trading mass from heterogeneous calendar families is time-aligned to the same closing execution window. SCD is built only from public institutional calendars and public price and volume data. It decomposes exactly into a self-mass term and a cross-clock overlap term; the normalized overlap term, which divides out scale, is the object of study. Across a fifteen-ETF daily panel (2016 to 2024, 32,130 ETF-days), the overlap term is non-spurious: its coefficient lies at the 0th percentile of a 1,000-iteration calendar-randomization null (two-sided p = 0.000), and a Monte Carlo power analysis confirms the design is well powered (minimum detectable effect 2.9 bp per standard deviation at 80 percent power). The headline finding is directional and was pre-registered against the opposite hypothesis: higher coordination predicts overnight return CONTINUATION, not the transitory reversal we pre-registered (overlap coefficient-5.03 bp per SD, t =-2.61 date-clustered,-2.83 ETF-clustered,-2.13 two-way). The effect is modern-era specific: it is absent over the full 1993 to 2024 history (t =-0.83), present in 2010 to 2024 (t =-2.46), and strongest in 2016 to 2024, consistent with the growth of leveraged ETFs and short-dated options raising clock-family overlap intensity. A complementary, signconsistent but statistically underpowered signal indicates the effect flips toward reversal at maximumcoordination quarter-end events (Phase 1 quarter-end subsample t = 2.56) and in individual stocks (quarter-end-down +48 bp per SD, t = 1.94). We pre-registered and rejected four distinct directional 'transient-pressure' hypotheses across five phases, committing each rejection as a first-class artifact, and we report a clean unconditional fact: the final thirty-minute window carries roughly fifteen percent of daily trading volume in eight percent of trading time. It is a real, non-spurious, ex ante coordination research whose directional signature favors information aggregation over transient pressure in liquid instruments; isolating the transient-pressure channel cleanly requires closing-auction imbalance data, which we identify as the binding constraint.

title: Who Owns the Stock Determines Where It Retraces: An Empirical Signature of the Cost-Penetration Partition

detail.title: Who Owns the Stock Determines Where It Retraces: An Empirical Signature of the Cost-Penetration Partition
detail.abstract: In a companion paper we proved that the Fibonacci retracement levels {0.236, 0.382, 0.500, 0.618, 0.786} arise structurally as the Cost Penetration Ratios (CPRs) of three canonical accumulation strategies on a geometric price sequence, and that the three strategies partition the retracement spectrum into disjoint sub-bands: harmonic-low, arithmetic-middle, geometric-high. That result was a theorem about weighted arithmetic; it made no empirical claim. This paper supplies the empirical claim. Using five years of daily price data for 38 US-listed equities, with each stock labeled by its SEC 13F institutional ownership fraction, we identify 230 significant upward swings (rally >= 20%) and compute the realized retracement depth following each. The cross-sectional regression of mean retracement on institutional ownership has slope -0.506 (HC1 robust p < 10^-6), R-squared = 0.429, Spearman rho = -0.691 (p < 10^-5); a three-bucket ANOVA gives F = 13.58 (p = 4.3 x 10^-5), with bucket means {0.742, 0.606, 0.491} tracking the theoretical CPR ordering E[1-CPR_D] > E[1-CPR_E] > E[1-CPR_G] exactly. Bootstrap and jackknife analyses confirm robustness: the OLS slope's 95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.69, -0.36] excludes zero, and no single stock changes the slope by more than 7%. The data thus support a structural reading of the cost-penetration partition: stock-level participant structure predicts the retracement regime. Institutional-dominated stocks behave consistently with the geometric (momentum-scaled) strategy; retail-dominated stocks behave consistently with the harmonic (dollar-cost-averaging) strategy.

detail.abstract:
Behind every instance of collapse across natural and artificial systems lies a single universal principle — when flow stops, life ends. Flow is generated by gradients — differences in concentration, voltage, or pressure — and ceases when these gradients are extinguished or pathways are blocked. From cell necrosis to stellar death, from organ failure to macroeconomic crisis, this paper identifies the structural commonality that has remained hidden behind interdisciplinary barriers and proposes a Five-Layer Architecture of circulatory system collapse.

Layer 1 addresses the cosmic origin and return of calcium (Where/Why). Layer 2 proposes that calcium functions as the physical execution code of the DNA blueprint (How). Layer 3 defines the six-phase life cycle from birth to return. Layer 4 formalizes the DTDMC collapse pathway and the physical basis for its repetition across domains (functional isomorphism). Layer 5 presents independent verification in the medical and economic domains. This paper does not directly verify each layer. As a framework paper, it presents the five-layer hierarchical structure, inter-layer logical connections, a verification roadmap, and falsification conditions. The overall structure is designed to satisfy the conditions required by Whewell's consilience of inductions and Kitcher's unification model — evidence from independent domains converging on a single pattern.

detail.abstract:
The phenomenon of structurally identical collapse pathways being observed in physically distinct domains is a recurring fact that modern science has repeatedly encountered. Microvascular calcification in the cardiovascular system, beta-amyloid aggregation in the nervous system, liquidity depletion in the financial system, biodiversity collapse in ecosystems — these are described independently across disciplines, yet the structural form of their pathways is strikingly similar. This similarity has, until now, been discussed largely at the level of analogy or metaphor; instances of rigorous mathematical and structural formalization that go beyond surface similarity to establish identity at the law-system level have been rare.

In prior work, the authors described aging and chronic disease in the medical domain in [P5a], and macroeconomic collapse in the economic domain in [P5b], independently using the same five-stage pathway law (DTDMC: Determinants–Trigger–Dual blockade–Manifestation–Collapse) and the same dual-blockade mathematical formalization (B* = CAM · DLT, where CAM is the Conductance Attenuation Metric — functional-signal blockade, and DLT is Deposition-induced Luminal Throttling — physical-channel blockade). Although the two domains have entirely different material substrates (calcium ions vs. money, vasculature vs. financial network), their constituent elements, relations, and consequences form a 1:1 correspondence, and they cohere as manifestations of the same upper physical principle [P0-G] — energy is converted into flow through gradients, and the moment the gradient vanishes, flow ceases (the E–∇–M three-term structure).

The present paper formalizes the observation left by these two independent verifications — that the two domains are described by the same law — as a structural proof of functional isomorphism. The proof level adopted by this paper is structural proof: it establishes isomorphism by presenting a complete 1:1 mapping of the (i) constituent elements, (ii) inter-element relations, (iii) governing laws, and (iv) invariants of the two domains. The structural proof does not pursue full categorical-morphism rigor, but it maintains a level of precision that can serve as the foundation for future categorical formalization.

This paper presents three layered laws. First Law: the DTDMC five stages are domain-invariant (Chapter 3). The three properties of [P3A] — order invariance, irreversible acceleration, and domain independence — are confirmed in both the medical domain of [P5a] and the economic domain of [P5b]. Second Law: the multiplicative structure B* = CAM · DLT is domain-invariant (Chapter 4). The mathematical formalization of [P3b] is shown to instantiate identically in both domains, with the three bases of the multiplicative structure (AND logic, additive counterexample, Poiseuille correspondence) confirmed as domain-neutral. Third Law: the E–∇–M three-term structure of [P0-G] is domain-invariant (Chapter 5). The principle that energy is converted into flow through gradients is shown to operate identically in both domains. The three laws together establish a hierarchical relation: the highest axiomatic layer (E–∇–M) induces the middle pathway layer (DTDMC), which is in turn mathematized by the concrete layer (B* = CAM · DLT).

Once the structural proof of these three laws is established, the authors' top-level proposition "Flow stops, life ends" is no longer a single-domain analogy but is shown — at the structural-proof level — to be a necessary consequence of the three laws. This paper occupies the structural-proof keystone of the authors' nine-paper portfolio and unifies the pathway-collapse research program. Chapters 6 and 7 discuss the boundaries of the proof and the conditions for extension to additional domains. Chapter 8 concludes that the central proposition of this paper is a theorem-level proposition derivable from the three laws above, and lays out a roadmap for future research.

detail.abstract:
Background: Motion artefact frequently renders brain MRI sequences non-diagnostic, prompting repeat acquisition and delayed reporting. Deep-learning correction has shown technical promise, but whether it improves sequence-level diagnostic usability in routine workflow remains insufficiently established.

Methods: We developed PERCEPT-Net, a deep-learning motion-correction model, and evaluated it in a multicentre study at three Chinese hospitals. The study included retrospective model development at Hospital 1, independent retrospective validation at Hospital 2, prospective paired multireader validation at Hospital 1 and Hospital 3, and an independent clean-input no-harm safety cohort. The prospective primary cohort included 188 patients contributing 241 T1- or T2-weighted sequence-level cases, each linked to a repeat acquisition within 30 min. Six blinded radiologists rated overall confidence on a 5-point scale. The prespecified primary endpoint was sequence-level diagnostic usability, defined by majority rating of 3 or higher. An exploratory shadow-mode workflow decision substudy was performed in the same prospective cohort to assess repeat-acquisition recommendations before and after corrected-output review.

Findings: Sequence-level diagnostic usability increased from 48·5% (117/241) before correction to 73·9% (178/241) after correction, an absolute gain of 25·4 percentage points (95% CI 20·8–27·3; p<0·001). Among 124 previously non-diagnostic sequences, 64 (51·6%) crossed the diagnostic-usability threshold after correction and three moved in the opposite direction, yielding a net gain of 61 diagnostically usable sequences. At the patient level, 62 of 106 patients (58·5%) with at least one initially non-diagnostic study sequence had at least one sequence rescued, and 51 (48·1%) had complete rescue of all initially non-diagnostic study sequences. In a prospective shadow-mode workflow decision substudy, corrected-output review reduced repeat-acquisition recommendations from 60·6% to 26·7% across 723 reader-sequence evaluations (absolute reduction, 33·9 percentage points; p<0·001), with consistent direction in a stricter yes-only sensitivity analysis. Radiomics stability was not restored, and clean-input testing showed measurable alteration of artefact-free images.

nterpretation: Deep-learning motion correction improved reader-assessed sequence-level diagnostic usability of motion-degraded brain MRI in a prospective paired multireader evaluation. However, corrected images were not interchangeable with motion-free originals for downstream quantitative use; radiomics stability was not restored, and this study did not establish lesion-level diagnostic accuracy, actual repeat-scan reduction, scanner-time savings, or patient-level clinical benefit. These findings support PERCEPT-Net as a conditionally triggered, human-reviewed adjunct for motion-degraded sequences, rather than as a quantitative surrogate, automated quality-control endpoint, or blanket correction step.

detail.abstract: Effective health measures are required to address health suffering caused by the devastating climate-induced diseases. Preference-based universal health coverage (UHC) is essential for creating equitable healthcare services accessible to everyone. However, current valuation practices of UHC for climate-induced diseases remain limited. This study aimed to measure the economic benefits of UHC. Using a cluster sampling technique, 716 respondents were selected from 22 villages in three coastal districts in Bangladesh. The study employed conditional logit, nested logit, and random parameter logit models to identify the essential attributes of UHC. The results showed that healthcare service availability, type of physician, renewal discount, special support for vulnerable groups, preventive services, nature of treatment coverage, number of climate-induced diseases covered, and annual payment for UHC have a statistically significant impact on the likelihood of selecting an alternative scenario of UHC. The MWTP estimates range from a high of 0.947 for the number of climate-induced diseases covered to a low of 0.004 for the type of physician. This disparity implies that coastal residents prioritize broader coverage for climate-related illnesses over the specific designation of a physician. Furthermore, the estimated CS of 0.058 suggests that the UHC scheme provides a net financial benefit to coastal populations. Consequently, the low initial preference for the UHC scheme in southwest coastal Bangladesh may not be misconstrued as low demand for UHC.
